claim: AgRP neurons increase motivation for food.
source: Agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons increase motivation for food, however, whether metabolic sensing of homeostatic state in AgRP neurons potentiates motivation by interacting with dopamine reward systems is unexplored.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact without supporting data in this manuscript, suggesting it is based on prior knowledge or citations.

claim: Crat deletion in AgRP neurons (KO) impaired ex vivo glucose-sensing.
source: Studies confirmed that Crat deletion in AgRP neurons (KO) impaired ex vivo glucose-sensing, as well as in vivo responses to peripheral glucose injection or repeated palatable food presentation and consumption.
evidence: The abstract states this was confirmed by studies, and the manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing reduced glucose-responsive neurons in KO mice.

claim: Crat deletion in AgRP neurons impaired in vivo responses to peripheral glucose injection.
source: Studies confirmed that Crat deletion in AgRP neurons (KO) impaired ex vivo glucose-sensing, as well as in vivo responses to peripheral glucose injection or repeated palatable food presentation and consumption.
evidence: The abstract states this was confirmed, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows differential AgRP activity responses to IP glucose in WT vs KO mice.

claim: Crat deletion in AgRP neurons impaired responses to repeated palatable food presentation and consumption.
source: Studies confirmed that Crat deletion in AgRP neurons (KO) impaired ex vivo glucose-sensing, as well as in vivo responses to peripheral glucose injection or repeated palatable food presentation and consumption.
evidence: The abstract states this was confirmed, and Figure 1 shows attenuated AgRP neural activity suppression in KO mice with repeated PB exposure.

claim: Impaired metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons reduced acute dopamine release (seconds) to palatable food consumption in the nucleus accumbens.
source: Impaired metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons reduced acute dopamine release (seconds) to palatable food consumption and during operant responding, as assessed by GRAB-DA photometry in the nucleus accumbens, but not the dorsal striatum.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 2 shows reduced NAc dopamine release in KO mice in response to PB chip presentation and contact.

claim: Impaired metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons reduced acute dopamine release during operant responding in the nucleus accumbens.
source: Impaired metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons reduced acute dopamine release (seconds) to palatable food consumption and during operant responding, as assessed by GRAB-DA photometry in the nucleus accumbens, but not the dorsal striatum.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 4 shows reduced NAc dopamine release in KO mice during rewarded nose pokes and pellet retrieval.

claim: Impaired metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons did not reduce acute dopamine release in the dorsal striatum.
source: Impaired metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons reduced acute dopamine release (seconds) to palatable food consumption and during operant responding, as assessed by GRAB-DA photometry in the nucleus accumbens, but not the dorsal striatum.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 5 shows no genotype differences in acute dorsal striatum dopamine release.

claim: Impaired metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons suppressed radiolabelled 18F-fDOPA accumulation after ~30 min in the dorsal striatum.
source: Impaired metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons suppressed radiolabelled 18F-fDOPA accumulation after ~30 min in the dorsal striatum but not the nucleus accumbens.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 6P shows reduced fDOPA uptake in dorsal striatum of KO mice at 30 min.

claim: Impaired metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons did not suppress radiolabelled 18F-fDOPA accumulation in the nucleus accumbens.
source: Impaired metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons suppressed radiolabelled 18F-fDOPA accumulation after ~30 min in the dorsal striatum but not the nucleus accumbens.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 6O shows no genotype differences in fDOPA uptake in ventral striatum.

claim: Impaired metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons suppressed motivated operant responding for sucrose rewards during fasting.
source: Impaired metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons suppressed motivated operant responding for sucrose rewards during fasting.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 3 shows reduced breakpoint, active nose pokes, and pellets collected in fasted KO mice.

claim: Metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons is required for the appropriate temporal integration and transmission of homeostatic hunger-sensing to dopamine signalling in the striatum.
source: Thus, metabolic-sensing in AgRP neurons is required for the appropriate temporal integration and transmission of homeostatic hunger-sensing to dopamine signalling in the striatum.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the experimental findings about differential temporal effects on NAc vs dorsal striatum dopamine.

claim: When food is abundant many prey species forage within known territories to reduce survival threats.
source: For example, when food is abundant many prey species forage within known territories to reduce survival threats (Sih, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sih, 1980.

claim: When food is scarce, animals are motivated to take greater risks and forage within unfamiliar territories to search for food.
source: Conversely, when food is scarce, animals are motivated to take greater risks and forage within unfamiliar territories to search for food (Whitham and Mathis, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Whitham and Mathis, 2000.

claim: Fasting biases reward systems to high caloric foods in humans.
source: Indeed, human evidence shows that fasting biases reward systems to high caloric foods (Goldstone et al., 2009; Cameron et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goldstone et al., 2009 and Cameron et al., 2014.

claim: AgRP neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus are a critical population of hunger-sensitive neurons that primarily function to increase appetite or conserve energy.
source: Agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARC) are a critical population of hunger-sensitive neurons that primarily function to increase appetite or conserve energy (Aponte et al., 2011; Gropp et al., 2005; Krashes et al., 2011; Luquet et al., 2005; Ruan et al., 2014; Siemian et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Aponte et al., 2011; Gropp et al., 2005; Krashes et al., 2011; Luquet et al., 2005; Ruan et al., 2014; Siemian et al., 2021.

claim: Hunger has been used for decades in behavioural neuroscience to improve performance and learning in operant tasks.
source: Intriguingly, hunger has been used for decades in behavioural neuroscience to improve performance and learning in operant tasks (Ramond, 1954).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ramond, 1954.

claim: AgRP neurons increase the willingness to work for food and food rewards to the same level as that seen in fasted mice.
source: AgRP neurons function within this framework by increasing the willingness to work for food and food rewards to the same level as that seen in fasted mice (Krashes et al., 2011; Atasoy et al., 2012; Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krashes et al., 2011; Atasoy et al., 2012; Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016.

claim: AgRP neurons influence motivation circuits.
source: Moreover, AgRP neurons influence motivation circuits (Alhadeff et al., 2019; Dietrich et al., 2012; Mazzone et al., 2020), with chemogenetic activation elevating dopamine release in response to food consumption (Alhadeff et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alhadeff et al., 2019; Dietrich et al., 2012; Mazzone et al., 2020.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of AgRP neurons elevates dopamine release in response to food consumption.
source: Moreover, AgRP neurons influence motivation circuits (Alhadeff et al., 2019; Dietrich et al., 2012; Mazzone et al., 2020), with chemogenetic activation elevating dopamine release in response to food consumption (Alhadeff et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alhadeff et al., 2019.

claim: AgRP neurons are most active during periods of energy deficit.
source: Since AgRP neurons are most active during periods of energy deficit (Baskin et al., 1999; Briggs et al., 2011; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Schwartz et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2011), we hypothesised that they transmit hunger-specific metabolic information to motivation circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baskin et al., 1999; Briggs et al., 2011; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Schwartz et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2011.

claim: Sensory cues that predict food availability and palatability rapidly suppress hunger-sensitive AgRP neuronal activity in hungry mice.
source: Sensory cues that predict food availability and palatability rapidly suppress hunger-sensitive AgRP neuronal activity in hungry mice (Betley et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Betley et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017.

claim: Post-ingestive caloric feedback is required to sustainably reduce AgRP neuronal activity.
source: Although this decrease in activity occurs prior to food consumption, post-ingestive caloric feedback is required to sustainably reduce AgRP neuronal activity (Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017.

claim: The reduction of AgRP neuronal activity correlates with the number of calories ingested.
source: Indeed, the reduction of AgRP neuronal activity correlates with the number of calories ingested and was not observed after repeated ingestion of a non-caloric sweetened gel (Su et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Su et al., 2017.

claim: The maintenance of normal AgRP activity in response to post-ingestive gastrointestinal feedback requires metabolic sensing of available calories in combination with gut-brain neural communication.
source: These studies highlight that the maintenance of normal AgRP activity in response to post-ingestive gastrointestinal feedback requires metabolic sensing of available calories in combination with gut-brain neural communication (Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017; Goldstein et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017; Goldstein et al., 2021.

claim: Carnitine acetyltransferase (Crat) in AgRP neurons is required as a molecular sensor for peripheral substrate utilisation during fasting and refeeding.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that carnitine acetyltransferase (Crat) in AgRP neurons was required as a molecular sensor for peripheral substrate utilisation during fasting and refeeding (Reichenbach et al., 2018c).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reichenbach et al., 2018c.

claim: Crat activity in AgRP neurons programmed a broad metabolic response of the AgRP proteome.
source: Moreover, Crat activity in AgRP neurons programmed a broad metabolic response of the AgRP proteome and was required to promote normal refeeding after fasting (Reichenbach et al., 2018c).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reichenbach et al., 2018c.

claim: Crat activity in AgRP neurons is required to promote normal refeeding after fasting.
source: Moreover, Crat activity in AgRP neurons programmed a broad metabolic response of the AgRP proteome and was required to promote normal refeeding after fasting (Reichenbach et al., 2018c).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reichenbach et al., 2018c.

claim: In WT mice, 48% of AgRP neurons were glucose-excited, 33% were glucose-inhibited, and 19% were glucose-insensitive.
source: In WT mice, 48% of cells (n = 10/21) were excited, 33% of cells (n = 7/21) were inhibited and 19% (n = 4/21) were insensitive to changes in extracellular glucose (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In KO mice, 28% of AgRP neurons were glucose-excited, 16% were glucose-inhibited, and 56% were glucose-insensitive.
source: In KO mice, the number of glucose-excited cells was reduced compared to WT, with only 28% classified as glucose-excited (n = 7/25). Similarly, the incidence of glucose-inhibited cells was reduced to 16% (n = 4/25) of the population compared to WT mice, with the majority of cells not responding to 5 mM glucose 56% (n = 14/25) and classified as glucose insensitive (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 81% of AgRP neurons in WT mice responded to glucose, whereas only 44% of AgRP neurons in KO mice responded to glucose.
source: In total 17/21 AgRP neurons responded to an increase in extracellular glucose in WT mice, whereas as only 11/25 AgRP neurons responded to glucose in KO mice, representing a decrease in glucose-responsive neurons (WT 81% vs KO 44%).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text based on the electrophysiology data.

claim: Peak action potential amplitude was significantly lower in KO AgRP neurons compared to WT.
source: We detected no differences in the fundamental electrophysiological properties of AgRP neurons including resting membrane potential (Figure 1A), input resistance (Figure 1B), spontaneous firing frequency (Figure 1C), although peak action potential amplitude was significantly lower in KO mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: No genotype-dependent changes in the frequency of spontaneous excitatory or inhibitory post-synaptic potentials were detected in AgRP neurons.
source: Similarly, no genotype-dependent changes in the frequency of spontaneous excitatory or inhibitory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs or IPSPs, respectively) were detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, C), indicating no differences in the external synaptic input onto AgRP neurons in WT compared to KO mice.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, C.

claim: Glucose injection suppressed AgRP activity in WT and KO mice; however, activity quickly returned to baseline levels in fasted WT but not KO mice.
source: Glucose injection suppressed AgRP activity in WT and KO mice; however, activity quickly returned to baseline levels in fasted WT but not KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1L.

claim: The fall in AgRP activity was similar in WT and KO mice in response to first PB exposure.
source: The fall in AgRP activity was similar in WT and KO mice in response to first PB exposure (Figure 1G–H), however, with repeated exposure across different sessions WT mice showed a greater suppression of activity relative to first exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; Figure 1L, Video 1), consistent with previous studies showing that the magnitude of activity suppression is proportional to calories consumed (Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1G–H.

claim: With repeated PB exposure, WT mice showed a greater suppression of AgRP activity relative to first exposure.
source: The fall in AgRP activity was similar in WT and KO mice in response to first PB exposure (Figure 1G–H), however, with repeated exposure across different sessions WT mice showed a greater suppression of activity relative to first exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; Figure 1L, Video 1), consistent with previous studies showing that the magnitude of activity suppression is proportional to calories consumed (Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Figure 1L.

claim: KO mice did not exhibit any further reduction in AgRP activity to repeated PB exposure.
source: Unlike WT mice, KO mice did not exhibit any further reduction in AgRP activity to repeated PB exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, Figure 1L, Video 2) and the reduction in AgRP neural activity in KO mice to repeated PB exposure was significantly attenuated compared to WT mice at all time points after PB exposure either in ad libitum-fed (Figure 1J–K) or fasted mice (Figure 1M–N).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and Figure 1L.

claim: The reduction in AgRP neural activity in KO mice to repeated PB exposure was significantly attenuated compared to WT mice in ad libitum-fed mice.
source: Unlike WT mice, KO mice did not exhibit any further reduction in AgRP activity to repeated PB exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, Figure 1L, Video 2) and the reduction in AgRP neural activity in KO mice to repeated PB exposure was significantly attenuated compared to WT mice at all time points after PB exposure either in ad libitum-fed (Figure 1J–K) or fasted mice (Figure 1M–N).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1J–K.

claim: The reduction in AgRP neural activity in KO mice to repeated PB exposure was significantly attenuated compared to WT mice in fasted mice.
source: Unlike WT mice, KO mice did not exhibit any further reduction in AgRP activity to repeated PB exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, Figure 1L, Video 2) and the reduction in AgRP neural activity in KO mice to repeated PB exposure was significantly attenuated compared to WT mice at all time points after PB exposure either in ad libitum-fed (Figure 1J–K) or fasted mice (Figure 1M–N).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1M–N.

claim: IP injection of ghrelin significantly increased food intake within 4 hr with no differences in genotype.
source: IP injection of ghrelin (1 mg/kg) significantly increased food intake within 4 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; main effect of ghrelin); however, no differences in genotype were observed.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: IP ghrelin significantly increased AgRP neural activity with no differences in genotype.
source: IP ghrelin significantly increased AgRP neural activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E; main effect of ghrelin); however, no differences in genotype were observed and the presentation of chow diet to ghrelin-injected mice produced an equal suppression in AgRP neural activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F-G; main effect of food access), again without differences between WT and KO mice.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: The presentation of chow diet to ghrelin-injected mice produced an equal suppression in AgRP neural activity without differences between WT and KO mice.
source: IP ghrelin significantly increased AgRP neural activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E; main effect of ghrelin); however, no differences in genotype were observed and the presentation of chow diet to ghrelin-injected mice produced an equal suppression in AgRP neural activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F-G; main effect of food access), again without differences between WT and KO mice.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F-G.

claim: No differences in anxiety-like behaviour were observed in the light-dark box or elevated-plus maze between WT and KO mice.
source: Finally, we observed no differences in anxiety-like behaviour in the light-dark box or elevated-plus maze (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I-P), although KO mice showed reduced locomotor activity in the elevated-plus maze but not light-dark box.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I-P.

claim: KO mice showed reduced locomotor activity in the elevated-plus maze but not light-dark box.
source: Finally, we observed no differences in anxiety-like behaviour in the light-dark box or elevated-plus maze (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I-P), although KO mice showed reduced locomotor activity in the elevated-plus maze but not light-dark box.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I-P.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of AgRP neurons modulates dopamine release in the NAc to food.
source: Previous studies show that chemogenetic activation of AgRP neurons modulates dopamine release in the NAc to food (Alhadeff et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alhadeff et al., 2019.

claim: A significant increase in dopamine release was observed in response to chow or a PB chip presentation when compared to wood dowel in both fed and fasted WT mice 0–30 s after placing the food or object into the cage.
source: We observed a significant increase in dopamine release in response to chow or a PB chip presentation when compared to wood dowel in both fed and fasted WT mice 0–30 s after placing the food or object into the cage (Figure 2D, E, H1; Videos 3–6).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2D, E, H and Videos 3–6.

claim: KO mice had significantly lower NAc dopamine release between 0 and 30 s after a non-food object or PB chip was placed in the cage compared to WT fed mice.
source: Strikingly, KO mice had significant lower NAc dopamine release between 0 and 30 s, as assessed by average z-score, after a non-food object or PB chip was placed in the cage compared to WT fed mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Average z-score was significantly reduced in fasted KO mice in response to chow and PB chip (0–30 s) when compared to WT fasted mice.
source: Average z-score was also significantly reduced in fasted KO mice in response to chow and PB chip (0–30 s) when compared to WT fasted mice (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: At 30–60 s after food or an object was placed in the cage, the average z-score was only significantly lower in KO in response to PB in the fed mice.
source: At 30–60 s after food or an object was placed in the cage, the average z-score was only significantly lower in KO in response to PB in the fed mice (Figure 2G and K), suggesting most of the differential effects occur within the first 30 s after presentation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2G and K.

claim: There was a significantly reduced dopamine response 0–30 s after contact with PB in KO compared to WT mice in both fed and fasted states.
source: Furthermore, we aligned the dopamine signal to first contact with the PB chip (Figure 2L and M) and showed that there was a significantly reduced dopamine response 0–30 s after contact with PB in KO compared to WT mice in both fed and fasted states (Figure 2O and P).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2O and P.

claim: No differences in dopamine release were observed in the 20 s prior to first contact or from 30 to 60 s after contact with PB.
source: No differences in dopamine release were observed in the 20 s prior to first contact or from 30 to 60 s after contact (Figure 2O and P).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2O and P.

claim: Time spent eating or time to first contact were not significantly different in WT and KO mice in fed or fasted state.
source: Time spent eating or time to first contact were not significantly different in WT and KO mice in fed or fasted state showing that these factors could not account for genotype differences in dopamine release in the NAc, although there was an expected main effect for fasting to increase overall time spent eating compared to fed mice, irrespective of genotype (Figure 2Q and R).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2Q and R.

claim: There was an expected main effect for fasting to increase overall time spent eating compared to fed mice, irrespective of genotype.
source: Time spent eating or time to first contact were not significantly different in WT and KO mice in fed or fasted state showing that these factors could not account for genotype differences in dopamine release in the NAc, although there was an expected main effect for fasting to increase overall time spent eating compared to fed mice, irrespective of genotype (Figure 2Q and R).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2Q and R.

claim: There were no differences in operant responding during FR sessions between WT and KO mice, indicating no differences in learning the operant task.
source: With this approach, there were no differences in operant responding during FR sessions (Figure 3C), indicating no differences in learning the operant task.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: During PR fed experiments, WT and KO mice displayed a similar breakpoint and total number of pellets collected.
source: During PR fed experiments, WT and KO mice displayed a similar breakpoint (Figure 3D) and total number of pellets collected (Figure 3E), however, during a fasted PR, KO mice showed a reduced breakpoint and total pellet consumption compared to WT mice (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: During a fasted PR, KO mice showed a reduced breakpoint and total pellet consumption compared to WT mice.
source: During PR fed experiments, WT and KO mice displayed a similar breakpoint (Figure 3D) and total number of pellets collected (Figure 3E), however, during a fasted PR, KO mice showed a reduced breakpoint and total pellet consumption compared to WT mice (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Active nose pokes during the fasted PR session were significantly lower in KO mice compared to WT.
source: Active (Figure 3F) but not inactive nose pokes (Figure 3G) during the fasted PR session were significantly lower in KO mice compared to WT, as well as pellets received during the progressive ratio session (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Inactive nose pokes during the fasted PR session were not significantly different between KO and WT mice.
source: Active (Figure 3F) but not inactive nose pokes (Figure 3G) during the fasted PR session were significantly lower in KO mice compared to WT, as well as pellets received during the progressive ratio session (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Pellets received during the fasted progressive ratio session were significantly lower in KO mice compared to WT.
source: Active (Figure 3F) but not inactive nose pokes (Figure 3G) during the fasted PR session were significantly lower in KO mice compared to WT, as well as pellets received during the progressive ratio session (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Active nose pokes and pellets collected only diverge around 6–8 hr after the beginning of fasting and the PR session.
source: Intriguingly, active nose pokes and pellets collected only diverge around 6–8 hr after the beginning of fasting and the PR session, similar to when food intake diverges after fasting as previously described (Reichenbach et al., 2018c; Reichenbach et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and references previous studies (Reichenbach et al., 2018c; Reichenbach et al., 2018b).

claim: In fed and fasted WT mice, a rewarded nose poke significantly increased NAc dopamine release 0–60 s after a poke event compared to 5 s prior to poke.
source: In fed and fasted WT mice, a rewarded nose poke significantly increased NAc dopamine release, as assessed by average z-score 0–60 s after a poke event compared to 5 s prior to poke (Figure 4D, H, F, G and J).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4D, H, F, G and J.

claim: A rewarded nose poke in fed or fasted KO mice did not significantly increase NAc dopamine release within 60 s of the nose poke compared to 5 s prior to poke.
source: However, a rewarded nose poke in fed or fasted KO mice did not significantly increase NAc dopamine release within 60 s of the nose poke compared to 5 s prior to poke (Figure 4E1, F, G and J).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4E, F, G and J.

claim: NAc dopamine release was significantly reduced during the 60-s period after a rewarded nose poke in KO compared to WT mice in both fed and fasted states.
source: In addition, NAc dopamine release was significantly reduced during the 60-s period after a rewarded nose poke in KO compared to WT mice in both fed and fasted states (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The time between nose pokes was lower in fasted mice compared to fed mice (main effect), but no genotype differences were observed.
source: The time between nose pokes was lower in fasted mice compared to fed mice (main effect; Figure 4P), but no genotype differences were observed.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4P.

claim: Dopamine release was significantly lower 0–10 s after pellet retrieval in KO mice compared to WT mice in both fed and fasted states.
source: We also analysed dopamine release aligned to pellet retrieval (Figure 4K, L, M, N, O, Q and R) and observed genotype differences in fed (Figure 4K and M), and fasted (Figure 4L and N) mice. Dopamine release was significantly lower 0–10 s after pellet retrieval in KO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 4K, L, M and N), but not different before pellet retrieval suggesting that reduced dopamine in KO is due to sucrose pellet consumption itself.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4K, L, M and N.

claim: Dopamine release was not different before pellet retrieval between WT and KO mice.
source: Dopamine release was significantly lower 0–10 s after pellet retrieval in KO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 4K, L, M and N), but not different before pellet retrieval suggesting that reduced dopamine in KO is due to sucrose pellet consumption itself.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4K, L, M and N.

claim: Time to pellet retrieval was significantly longer in fed KO mice compared to fed WT mice.
source: Interestingly, time to pellet retrieval was significantly longer in fed KO mice compared to fed WT mice (Figure 4Q).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4Q.

claim: Neural encoding of non-caloric and caloric solutions is differentially processed in the NAc and dorsal striatum respectively.
source: Previous studies have suggested that neural encoding of non-caloric and caloric solutions is differentially processed in the NAc and dorsal striatum respectively (Tellez et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tellez et al., 2016.

claim: A main effect for a PB chip to acutely increase dopamine release in the dorsal striatum 0–30 s and 30–60 s after food or object presentation was observed, but there were no significant genotype differences in either the fed or fasted state.
source: Although we observed a main effect for a PB chip to acutely increase dopamine release in the dorsal striatum 0–30 s and 30–60 s after food or object presentation, there were no significant genotype differences in either the fed or fasted state (Figure 5D–K).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5D–K.

claim: No genotype differences in contact with PB in fed or fasted mice were observed at any time point (−20–0, 0–30, 30–60 s) when data were aligned to contact with PB.
source: When data were aligned to contact with PB, we observed no genotype differences in contact with PB in fed or fasted mice at any time point (−20–0, 0–30, 30–60 s; Figure 5L, M and S).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5L, M and S.

claim: A main effect of time to increase dopamine release at 0–30 s in fed and fasted mice was observed independent from genotype.
source: However, we observed a main effect of time to increase dopamine release at 0–30 s in fed and fasted mice (Figure 5O and P) independent from genotype showing that PB consumption elicits an acute increase in dopamine release in the dorsal striatum.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5O and P.

claim: No differences in time to contact with a PB chip or time spent eating a PB chip were observed between WT and KO mice.
source: Similar to data collected from the NAc experiments, no differences in time to contact with a PB chip or time spent eating a PB chip (5Q, R) were observed.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5Q, R.

claim: Aligning dorsal striatal dopamine to nose pokes showed a significant increase in dopamine release 0–10 seconds after a rewarded nose poke in both fed and fasted mice, independent from genotype.
source: Aligning dorsal striatal dopamine to nose pokes showed a significant increase in dopamine release 0–10 seconds after a rewarded nose poke in both fed and fasted mice, independent from genotype (main effect of time; p < 0.05; Figure 6D–I).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6D–I.

claim: When aligned to pellet retrieval, dorsal striatal dopamine peaked immediately prior to retrieval with no significant genotype differences in average z-score prior to or after pellet retrieval.
source: When aligned to pellet retrieval, dorsal striatal dopamine peaked immediately prior to retrieval (Figure 6J–K) with no significant genotype differences in average z-score prior to or after pellet retrieval (Figure 6L and M).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6J–K, L and M.

claim: No differences in fDOPA uptake were observed in ventral (nucleus accumbens) and dorsal striatum in fasted mice without reward presentation, suggesting impaired metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons does not affect baseline uptake parameters.
source: First, we measured dynamic basal dopamine uptake in ventral (nucleus accumbens) and dorsal striatum in fasted mice without reward presentation and observed no differences in fDOPA uptake (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) suggesting impaired metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons does not affect baseline uptake parameters.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In response to PB chip consumption, an increase in fDOPA accumulation 30 min after starting was detected in the dorsal striatum of WT but not in KO mice.
source: However, in response to PB chip consumption, we detected an increase in fDOPA accumulation 30 min after starting in the dorsal striatum of WT but not in KO mice (Figure 6P) and no differences in the ventral striatum (Figure 6O).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6P.

claim: No differences in fDOPA accumulation were observed in the ventral striatum in response to PB chip consumption.
source: However, in response to PB chip consumption, we detected an increase in fDOPA accumulation 30 min after starting in the dorsal striatum of WT but not in KO mice (Figure 6P) and no differences in the ventral striatum (Figure 6O).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6O.

claim: Crat deletion from myocytes diminishes the switch from fatty acid metabolism to glucose metabolism after pyruvate administration.
source: An important role for Crat in metabolic sensing is supported by studies deleting Crat from myocytes, as this diminishes the switch from fatty acid metabolism to glucose metabolism after pyruvate administration (Muoio et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Muoio et al., 2012.

claim: The first presentation of PB to WT and KO mice produces a similar reduction in AgRP neural activity suggesting normal integration of sensory and taste information, in the absence of post-ingestive interoceptive information.
source: Intriguingly, in our studies, the first presentation of PB to WT and KO mice produces a similar reduction in AgRP neural activity suggesting normal integration of sensory and taste information, in the absence of post-ingestive interoceptive information.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 1G–H.

claim: The subsequent fall in AgRP activity from WT mice after initial PB consumption shows that WT mice integrate additional interoceptive information based on post-ingestive feedback from PB consumption.
source: The subsequent fall in AgRP activity from WT mice after initial PB consumption shows that WT mice integrate additional interoceptive information based on post-ingestive feedback from PB consumption.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: KO mice do not show any greater suppression of AgRP neural activity with repeated PB exposure and consumption.
source: However, KO mice do not show any greater suppression of AgRP neural activity with repeated PB exposure and consumption.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The consumption of caloric gels, but not non caloric gels, is required for the sustained suppression of AgRP neuron activity, the magnitude of which is proportional to the calories obtained.
source: Su et al demonstrated that the consumption of caloric gels, but not non caloric gels, is required for the sustained suppression of AgRP neuron activity, the magnitude of which is proportional to the calories obtained.
evidence: This claim is supported by a reference to Su et al., 2017.

claim: The caloric value of a gel was learnt in a single trial.
source: In these studies the caloric value of a gel was learnt in a single trial (Su et al., 2017), similar to the response seen in WT mice after first exposure to PB in our studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Su et al., 2017.

claim: The majority of inhibitory input to AgRP neurons comes from GABAergic leptin-receptor expressing DMH (DMHLEPR) neurons.
source: The majority of inhibitory input to AgRP neurons comes from GABAergic leptin-receptor expressing DMH (DMHLEPR) neurons (Garfield et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Garfield et al., 2016.

claim: DMHLEPR neurons provide inhibitory input to AgRP neurons in response to sensory cues but with only a minimal response to metabolic signals.
source: Importantly, DMHLEPR neurons provide inhibitory input to AgRP neurons in response to sensory cues but with only a minimal response to metabolic signals (Berrios et al., 2021), arguing against the possibility of altered inhibitory input in AgRP neurons from KO mice in our study.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berrios et al., 2021.

claim: Altered mitochondrial glucose metabolism, as observed after crat deletion, affects GABA metabolism.
source: It is also possible that Crat deletion from AgRP neurons alters the post-synaptic response to GABAergic inhibitory inputs since altered mitochondrial glucose metabolism, as observed after crat deletion, affects GABA metabolism (Cavalcanti-de-Albuquerque et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cavalcanti-de-Albuquerque et al., 2021.

claim: IP glucose injection suppressed AgRP neural activity in WT and KO mice, however activity quickly returned to pre-injection levels in WT fasted but not KO fasted mice.
source: Similar to recently published observations (Goldstein et al., 2021), IP glucose injection suppressed AgRP neural activity in WT and KO mice, however activity quickly returned to pre-injection levels in WT fasted but not KO fasted mice.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Goldstein et al., 2021.

claim: The integration of calorie information is required to sustain suppressed AgRP neural activity.
source: Given that the integration of calorie information is required to sustain suppressed AgRP neural activity (Chen et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017), our data highlight that calorie availability from IP glucose administration was insufficient to sustain the suppression of AgRP neural activity in fasted WT mice and activity returned to pre-glucose levels to encourage further food seeking.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017.

claim: Calorie availability from IP glucose administration was insufficient to sustain the suppression of AgRP neural activity in fasted WT mice and activity returned to pre-glucose levels to encourage further food seeking.
source: Given that the integration of calorie information is required to sustain suppressed AgRP neural activity (Chen et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017), our data highlight that calorie availability from IP glucose administration was insufficient to sustain the suppression of AgRP neural activity in fasted WT mice and activity returned to pre-glucose levels to encourage further food seeking.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Although fasted KO mice reduced activity in response to IP glucose injection, AgRP activity did not return to baseline levels indicating an inability to sense further calorie need.
source: Although fasted KO mice reduced activity in response to IP glucose injection, AgRP activity did not return to baseline levels indicating an inability to sense further calorie need.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons is required to potentiate acute dopamine release in the NAc.
source: Thus, metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons is required to potentiate acute dopamine release in the NAc, extending previous observations that artificial activation of AgRP neurons increases dopamine release in response to food (Alhadeff et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 2, with a citation to Alhadeff et al., 2019.

claim: The motivation to obtain food is associated with chemo- or opto-genetic activation of AgRP neurons.
source: Although the motivation to obtain food is associated with chemo- or opto-genetic activation of AgRP neurons (Krashes et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2016), our studies show metabolic sensing of homeostatic state is required for translating low energy availability into a dopamine-driven motivational action to consume sucrose.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krashes et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Metabolic sensing of homeostatic state is required for translating low energy availability into a dopamine-driven motivational action to consume sucrose.
source: Although the motivation to obtain food is associated with chemo- or opto-genetic activation of AgRP neurons (Krashes et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2016), our studies show metabolic sensing of homeostatic state is required for translating low energy availability into a dopamine-driven motivational action to consume sucrose.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Dopamine release increased prior to pellet retrieval in the NAc consistent with FED3-motor activity acting as an auditory cue for pellet delivery.
source: In the NAc, dopamine release increased prior to pellet retrieval consistent with FED3-motor activity acting as an auditory cue for pellet delivery, given the well-known role of cue-induced dopamine release in the NAc (Schiffer et al., 2009; Covey and Cheer, 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 4, with citations to Schiffer et al., 2009; Covey and Cheer, 2019.

claim: Cue-evoked dopamine release in the NAc reflects expected dopamine-mediated reinforcement rather than the actual magnitude of dopamine neuronal activation.
source: Intriguingly, cue-evoked dopamine release in the NAc reflects expected dopamine-mediated reinforcement rather than the actual magnitude of dopamine neuronal activation (Covey and Cheer, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Covey and Cheer, 2019.

claim: There were no differences in average z-score prior to pellet retrieval between WT and KO mice.
source: There were no differences in average z-score prior to pellet retrieval, however average z-score was reduced after pellet retrieval in KO mice under fasted conditions.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Average z-score was reduced after pellet retrieval in KO mice under fasted conditions.
source: There were no differences in average z-score prior to pellet retrieval, however average z-score was reduced after pellet retrieval in KO mice under fasted conditions.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons does not influence the response to the reward predicting cue, but to the reward itself, which is driven by taste and caloric value.
source: These observations show that metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons does not influence the response to the reward predicting cue, but to the reward itself, which is driven by taste and caloric value, as previously described (Chen et al., 2015; Goldstein et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 4, with citations to Chen et al., 2015; Goldstein et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2019.

claim: The combination of reduced breakpoint responding and lower dopamine release in the NAc to pellet retrieval is consistent with the known role of NAc dopamine release to drive food seeking.
source: The combination of reduced breakpoint responding and lower dopamine release in the NAc to pellet retrieval is consistent with the known role of NAc dopamine release to drive food seeking (Roitman et al., 2004) and to assign an appropriate investment of effort to the available reward (Hamid et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2013; Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to Roitman et al., 2004; Hamid et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2013; Mohebi et al., 2019.

claim: NAc dopamine release drives food seeking.
source: The combination of reduced breakpoint responding and lower dopamine release in the NAc to pellet retrieval is consistent with the known role of NAc dopamine release to drive food seeking (Roitman et al., 2004) and to assign an appropriate investment of effort to the available reward (Hamid et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2013; Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roitman et al., 2004.

claim: NAc dopamine release assigns an appropriate investment of effort to the available reward.
source: The combination of reduced breakpoint responding and lower dopamine release in the NAc to pellet retrieval is consistent with the known role of NAc dopamine release to drive food seeking (Roitman et al., 2004) and to assign an appropriate investment of effort to the available reward (Hamid et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2013; Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hamid et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2013; Mohebi et al., 2019.

claim: In the dorsal striatum, dopamine ramping was observed prior to pellet retrieval without any genotype differences, which dropped to baseline soon after pellet retrieval.
source: In the dorsal striatum, dopamine ramping was observed prior to pellet retrieval without any genotype differences, which dropped to baseline soon after pellet retrieval consistent with previous reports (London et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 6, with a citation to London et al., 2018.

claim: Studies in humans show palatable food elicits an immediate orosensory dopamine response and a delayed dorsal striatum dopamine response.
source: With photometry, we were unable to detect any differences in dopamine release in the dorsal striatum yet studies in humans show palatable food elicits an immediate orosensory dopamine response and a delayed dorsal striatum dopamine response (Thanarajah et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thanarajah et al., 2019.

claim: Impaired metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons causes an acute attenuation of dopamine release in the NAc but not the dorsal striatum.
source: Thus, we have identified an interesting separation in the temporal relationship of metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons and dopamine release in the NAc or dorsal striatum. Impaired metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons causes an acute attenuation of dopamine release in the NAc but not the dorsal striatum whereas it causes a longer term attenuation in the dorsal striatum but not the ventral striatum, which encompasses the NAc.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figures 2, 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Impaired metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons causes a longer term attenuation of dopamine in the dorsal striatum but not the ventral striatum.
source: Thus, we have identified an interesting separation in the temporal relationship of metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons and dopamine release in the NAc or dorsal striatum. Impaired metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons causes an acute attenuation of dopamine release in the NAc but not the dorsal striatum whereas it causes a longer term attenuation in the dorsal striatum but not the ventral striatum, which encompasses the NAc.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figures 2, 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Disrupting peripheral glucose oxidation suppresses dorsal striatum dopamine efflux during sugar intake.
source: For example, disrupting peripheral glucose oxidation suppresses dorsal striatum dopamine efflux during sugar intake (Tellez et al., 2013) and we have previously observed impaired glucose oxidation in response to refeeding after fasting in mice lacking Crat in AgRP neurons (Reichenbach et al., 2018c; Reichenbach et al., 2018b; Reichenbach et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tellez et al., 2013.

claim: Impaired glucose oxidation was observed in response to refeeding after fasting in mice lacking Crat in AgRP neurons.
source: For example, disrupting peripheral glucose oxidation suppresses dorsal striatum dopamine efflux during sugar intake (Tellez et al., 2013) and we have previously observed impaired glucose oxidation in response to refeeding after fasting in mice lacking Crat in AgRP neurons (Reichenbach et al., 2018c; Reichenbach et al., 2018b; Reichenbach et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reichenbach et al., 2018c; Reichenbach et al., 2018b; Reichenbach et al., 2018a.

claim: AgRP neurons respond to sensory cues within seconds yet require a slightly longer time frame (~minutes) to respond effectively to post-ingestive signals from the gut.
source: Moreover, AgRP neurons respond to sensory cues within seconds yet require a slightly longer time frame (~minutes) to respond effectively to post-ingestive signals from the gut, such as nutrients and hormones released into the blood or via neural pathways (Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017; Goldstein et al., 2021; Bai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Su et al., 2017; Beutler et al., 2017; Goldstein et al., 2021; Bai et al., 2019.

claim: Impaired metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons affects both the immediate acute response to reward consumption, via dopamine signalling in the NAc, as well as a slower response, which involves the integration of post-ingestive signals of calorie content in regions such as the dorsal striatum.
source: Thus, we predict that impaired metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons affects both the immediate acute response to reward consumption, via dopamine signalling in the NAc, as well as a slower response, which involves the integration of post-ingestive signals of calorie content in regions such as the dorsal striatum.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a prediction based on the experimental findings.

claim: Dopamine release in the dorsal striatum depends on calorie content, independent from taste, and is modulated by direct calorie infusion into the gut and gut-derived vagal afferents.
source: In support of this, dopamine release in the dorsal striatum depends on calorie content, independent from taste, and is modulated by direct calorie infusion into the gut and gut-derived vagal afferents (Tellez et al., 2016; de Araujo et al., 2008; Han et al., 2016; Han et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tellez et al., 2016; de Araujo et al., 2008; Han et al., 2016; Han et al., 2018.

claim: Both short term NAc dopamine release and longer-term dorsal striatum dopamine release may be required to manifest a behavioural change in motivation, both of which require metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons.
source: Furthermore, we predict that both short term NAc dopamine release and longer-term dorsal striatum dopamine release may be required to manifest a behavioural change in motivation, both of which require metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a prediction based on the experimental findings.

claim: NAc dopamine release to a rewarded nose poke is lower in both fed and fasted KO mice.
source: This comes from our observations that NAc dopamine release to a rewarded nose poke is lower in both fed and fasted KO mice, however reduced motivation for sucrose pellets in the PR session only manifests 6 hr into the fasted period.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Reduced motivation for sucrose pellets in the PR session only manifests 6 hr into the fasted period in KO mice.
source: This comes from our observations that NAc dopamine release to a rewarded nose poke is lower in both fed and fasted KO mice, however reduced motivation for sucrose pellets in the PR session only manifests 6 hr into the fasted period.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Changes in fDOPA accumulation in the dorsal striatum were only observed in mice fasted overnight.
source: Indeed, we only observed changes in fDOPA accumulation in the dorsal striatum in mice fasted overnight.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and is based on the data shown in Figure 6P.

claim: Artificial activation of AgRP neurons increases VTA dopamine activity.
source: Although artificial activation of AgRP neurons increases VTA dopamine activity (Mazzone et al., 2020), an unanswered question remains, as to how AgRP neurons influence mesolimbic dopamine signalling.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mazzone et al., 2020.

claim: Very few, if any, AgRP terminals are found in the adult VTA.
source: Given that very few, if any, AgRP terminals are found in the adult VTA (Dietrich et al., 2012) and the slow nature of AgRP activity at the MC4R (Krashes et al., 2013), it seems more likely that the effects of AgRP neurons on mesolimbic dopamine activity is driven through either NPY or GABA release at downstream targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dietrich et al., 2012.

claim: AgRP activity at the MC4R is slow in nature.
source: Given that very few, if any, AgRP terminals are found in the adult VTA (Dietrich et al., 2012) and the slow nature of AgRP activity at the MC4R (Krashes et al., 2013), it seems more likely that the effects of AgRP neurons on mesolimbic dopamine activity is driven through either NPY or GABA release at downstream targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krashes et al., 2013.

claim: The effects of AgRP neurons on mesolimbic dopamine activity is likely driven through either NPY or GABA release at downstream targets.
source: Given that very few, if any, AgRP terminals are found in the adult VTA (Dietrich et al., 2012) and the slow nature of AgRP activity at the MC4R (Krashes et al., 2013), it seems more likely that the effects of AgRP neurons on mesolimbic dopamine activity is driven through either NPY or GABA release at downstream targets.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculation based on cited evidence.

claim: NPY release is required for the ongoing ability of AgRP neurons to drive positive reinforcement and hunger signalling after the suppression of AgRP neuronal firing.
source: NPY release is required for the ongoing ability of AgRP neurons to drive positive reinforcement and hunger signalling after the suppression of AgRP neuronal firing (Chen et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019), suggesting it is the prime candidate to modulate dopamine release in NAc.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019.

claim: NPY is the prime candidate to modulate dopamine release in NAc.
source: NPY release is required for the ongoing ability of AgRP neurons to drive positive reinforcement and hunger signalling after the suppression of AgRP neuronal firing (Chen et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019), suggesting it is the prime candidate to modulate dopamine release in NAc.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculation based on cited evidence.

claim: Metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons is required to transmit interoceptive metabolic information into dopamine release in the NAc and dorsal striatum, albeit over different time frames.
source: In summary, we show that metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons is required to transmit interoceptive metabolic information into dopamine release in the NAc and dorsal striatum, albeit over different time frames, and to increase motivated behaviour for sucrose rewards.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the Discussion, synthesizing the experimental findings.

claim: Metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons is required to increase motivated behaviour for sucrose rewards.
source: In summary, we show that metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons is required to transmit interoceptive metabolic information into dopamine release in the NAc and dorsal striatum, albeit over different time frames, and to increase motivated behaviour for sucrose rewards.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the Discussion, synthesizing the experimental findings from Figure 3.
